Empirical Research Plan: Smoke from the 1997 Indonesian Forest Fires and Early-Life Mortality  

-------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension embedded in a two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) panel.  

Why it fits  
• Sharp, short-lived nationwide “event” (Aug–Nov 1997 fires) that differentially raised particulate matter across space.  
• Monthly panel of 3,751 sub-districts for 18 months gives rich pre- and post-periods.  
• Continuous treatment intensity (satellite aerosol index) can be interacted with a post-fire dummy to create a “dose DID.”  
• Gestation calendars allow us to translate month-level pollution into cohort-specific in-utero and post-natal exposure windows.  
• Event-study coefficients on leads validate parallel-trend assumption and pinpoint most damaging gestational month.  

Equation (conceptual)  
log(CohortSize)_{i,b} = α_i + λ_b + Σ_{k=-12}^{+12} β_k Smoke_{i,b+k} × 1{k} + X'_{i,b}γ + ε_{i,b}  

α_i = sub-district FE, λ_b = birth-month FE. Smoke_{i,b+k} gives pollution k months relative to birth. The β_k trace the event study.  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
Smoke_{i,m}: monthly median TOMS aerosol index (or # high-smoke days ≥ AI = 1.5) within 100 km of sub-district i in calendar month m.  

Stage-specific cumulative exposures (main specifications)  
In-utero: IU_{i,b} = Σ_{τ=-9}^{-1} Smoke_{i,b+τ}  
Post-natal (0–11 m): PN_{i,b} = Σ_{τ=0}^{11} Smoke_{i,b+τ}  

Control group  
Sub-district-cohorts with low or zero smoke in the relevant window constitute the counterfactual. Because treatment is continuous, identification comes from within-time cross-sectional variation and within-place time variation.  

Timing  
Event date = Aug 1997. “Post” dummy equals 1 for calendar months Aug–Nov 1997 and, for gestation windows, for any conception month whose pregnancy overlaps Aug–Nov 1997.  

No RDD is used; no running variable.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends: In absence of smoke, high- and low-smoke sub-districts would have evolved similarly in cohort survival. Plausibility: pre-fire months (Dec 1996–Jul 1997) allow a graphic and statistical test.  

A2. Exogenous smoke intensity: Conditional on fixed effects and contemporaneous weather controls, spatial smoke gradients are driven by wind + fire location, not local health investments or parental behavior. Institutional context (lightning-fast spread, weak firefighting) supports plausibility.  

A3. Stable population composition: No large, selective migration of pregnant women or infants within 18 months. Census mobility questions suggest low short-run moves; will be probed in robustness.  

A4. No simultaneous shocks differentially correlated with smoke after conditioning on month*island FE and rainfall (e.g., local financial-crisis severity).  

A5. Correct gestation alignment: Birth-month minus nine approximates conception; mis-dating is classical and attenuates estimates.  

4. Main Threats and Remedies  

T1. Asian Financial Crisis confounds (income collapse, food prices).  
Remedy: Add sub-district-specific linear trends; control for monthly log food-CPI × province FE, rainfall, fires-to-economic-shock IV (see robustness).  

T2. Selective fertility (parents postpone conception because of smoke; “missing children” due to fewer pregnancies not fetal loss).  
Remedy: a) Include sub-district-month counts of conceptions conceived 9 months later to isolate fertility response; b) run sex-ratio and parity-specific tests; c) bound analysis using upper-bound fertility adjustment (Abadie et al. 2020 style).  

T3. Measurement error in satellite aerosol index.  
Remedy: Re-estimate with (i) number of fire hot-spots within 50 km, (ii) count of calm-wind days × hot-spots as an IV for aerosol index. Compare coefficients.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# -------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # TWFE regressions
library(ggplot2)      # plotting
# -------------------------------------------

# 1. Load data
poll   <- fread("subdistrict_month_pollution.csv")  # i, month, smoke
cohort <- fread("subdistrict_birthcohorts.csv")     # i, birth_month, cohort_size
weather<- fread("rainfall_month.csv")               # rainfall
econ   <- fread("cpi_month.csv")                    # food CPI

# 2. Merge to subdistrict-birthmonth panel
setkey(poll, subdist_id, month)
setkey(cohort, subdist_id, birth_month)

panel <- merge(cohort, poll, by.x = c("subdist_id","birth_month"),
               by.y = c("subdist_id","month"), all.x = TRUE)

# 3. Build gestation and postnatal exposure
for (lag in -9:11){
  lagname <- paste0("smoke_lag",sprintf("%02d",lag))
  panel[, (lagname) := shift(smoke, n = -lag, type = "lead"), by = subdist_id]
}

panel[, IU := rowSums(.SD, na.rm = TRUE), .SDcols = paste0("smoke_lag",sprintf("%02d",-9:-1))]
panel[, PN := rowSums(.SD, na.rm = TRUE), .SDcols = paste0("smoke_lag",sprintf("%02d",0:11))]

# 4. Controls
panel <- merge(panel, weather, by = c("subdist_id","birth_month"))
panel <- merge(panel, econ,    by = "birth_month")
panel[, log_cpi := log(food_cpi)]

# 5. Main regression (TWFE, clustered at sub-district)
est_main <- feols(log(cohort_size) ~ IU + PN + rainfall + log_cpi |
                    subdist_id + birth_month, data = panel, cluster = ~subdist_id)

summary(est_main)

# 6. Event-study (gestational month-specific)
gest_vars <- paste0("smoke_lag", sprintf("%02d",-12:12))
form_es   <- as.formula(
  paste0("log(cohort_size) ~ ", paste(gest_vars, collapse="+"),
         " | subdist_id + birth_month"))
est_es <- feols(form_es, data = panel, cluster = ~subdist_id)

iplot(est_es, ci = TRUE, ref.line = 0)

# 7. Robustness: IV using hot-spots * calm-wind as instrument
library(AER)
panel[, instr := hotspots_calmwind]  # assume created earlier
iv_main <- feols(log(cohort_size) ~ 1 | subdist_id + birth_month | 
                 (IU ~ instr), data = panel, cluster = ~subdist_id)
summary(iv_main)
```

6. Expected Results  

Direction: Higher particulate exposure lowers surviving cohort size.  

Magnitude (rough prior): One standard deviation increase in in-utero smoke (≈10 high-smoke days or AI ≈ 1) reduces surviving cohort size by 2–5 percent. Post-natal coefficient negative but about half the size of the in-utero effect.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  

C1. Pre-treatment parallel trends visually/statistically supported … 1  
C2. No contemporaneous treatments correlated with smoke after controls … 0.5  
C3. No spillovers/contamination across sub-districts … 0.5  
C4. Stable unit composition (no selective migration) … 0.5  
C5. Treatment exogeneity conditional on FE and weather … 1  

Overall ≈ 3.5 / 5 – credible but not bullet-proof.
